facts.statement: Fossils of Iniopteryx have been found in the U.S. states of Nebraska and Indiana.
facts.quote: Fossils of Iniopteryx are known from the U.S. states of Nebraska and Indiana.

facts.statement: The largest known specimens of Iniopteryx measure between 30 and 35 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: PF6678 and PF6645 are the largest specimens of Iniopteryx and are between 30 and 35 centimeters in length.

facts.statement: The internal skeleton of Iniopteryx was composed of calcified cartilage.
facts.quote: The internal skeleton of Iniopteryx was made up of calcified cartilage.

facts.statement: Iniopteryx had large eyes positioned behind the nasal openings, supported by sclerotic rings made of calcified cartilage.
facts.quote: The eye sockets were positioned behind the nasal openings, and housed large eyes which had sclerotic rings made up of calcified cartilage.

facts.statement: Iniopteryx possessed small, hook-shaped denticles in its mouth that may have been composed of orthodentine.
facts.quote: The dentition of Iniopteryx consisted of small denticles with hook-shaped cusps, which may have been made up of orthodentine.

facts.statement: Male Iniopteryx had a large, recurved denticle on their pelvic fin that functioned as a tenaculum, similar to those found in chimaeras.
facts.quote: The basipterygium of male Iniopteryx also supported a large, recurved denticle that acted as a tenaculum similar in function (but not anatomy) to that of chimaeras.

facts.statement: Iniopteryx lacked vertebral centra and had an entirely uncalcified notochord, unlike modern chimaeras which have calcified rings.
facts.quote: The vertebrae of Iniopteryx lack a vertebral centra, a similar condition to modern chimaeroids; however, unlike living chimaeras, Iniopteryx lacked a vertebral column made up of calcified rings and had an entirely uncalcified notochord.

facts.statement: The large, nape-positioned pectoral fins were likely the primary means of locomotion for Iniopteryx.
facts.quote: The large size and position of the pectoral fins in Iniopteryx suggests that they were the primary means of locomotion.

facts.statement: Researchers compared the movement of Iniopteryx's pectoral fins to the flight stroke of a bird or the forelimbs of a sea turtle.
facts.quote: The pectoral fins likely would have moved vertically in a similar manner to the flight stroke of a bird, and were compared to the forelimbs of a sea turtle by Zangerl and Case.

facts.statement: Iniopteryx is the type genus of the Iniopterygiformes, a group of cartilaginous fish debated as either stem-holocephalans or stem-group chondrichthyans related to Elasmobranchii and Holocephali.
facts.quote: Iniopteryx is the type genus of the Iniopterygiformes, a clade of chondrichthyans variously considered as stem-holocephalans or as stem-group chondrichthyans sister to the clade containing Elasmobranchii and Holocephali.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Iniopteryx had a holostylic jaw suspension, as later research contradicted the original description that claimed the upper jaws were fused to the braincase.
facts.quote: However, later research by paleontologist Barbara J. Stahl found that the palatoquadrates were not fused to the braincase, and that the jaw suspension was not holostylic.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Iniopteryx had small, fragile teeth that limited its diet to soft food.
facts.quote: The teeth of Iniopteryx were small and fragile, which Zangerl and Case suggest limited it to a diet of soft food.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence from stomach infills in specimens PF6672 and PF6646 shows that Iniopteryx ate arthropod exoskeletons, conodonts, and plant matter.
facts.quote: A number of articulated specimens preserve an infill of the mineral hydroxyapatite in the stomach cavity, and in some specimens (PF6672 and PF6646) this infill contains arthropod exoskeletons, conodonts, and plant matter.

facts.statement: Researchers theorize that the low number of female fossils compared to males was caused by higher predation on females, while males used their denticle-covered pectoral fins for defense.
facts.quote: The authors theorized that this may have been caused by an increased rate of predation among the females, as the males could have used their denticle-covered pectoral fins for defense.

facts.statement: Iniopteryx is an extinct genus of holocephalans that appeared in the Carboniferous and disappeared by the end of the Permian.
facts.quote: Iniopteryx es un género extinto de holocéfalos que apareció en el Carbonífero y desapareció a finales del Pérmico.

facts.statement: Fossils of Iniopteryx have been found abundantly only in Pennsylvania, North America.
facts.quote: Sus fósiles solamente han sido encontrados con abundancia en Pensilvania (Estados Unidos), en Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Iniopteryx was characterized by having fins similar to those of flying fish.
facts.quote: Se caracterizaba por tener aletas parecidas a las de los peces voladores.

facts.statement: Iniopteryx belongs to the order Iniopterygia.
facts.quote: ordo: Iniopterygia

facts.statement: Iniopteryx is classified within the class Chondrichthyes.
facts.quote: classis: Chondrichthyes

facts.statement: Iniopteryx lived from the Moscovian to the Kasimovian stages, between 315.2 and 303.7 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Moscovian to Kasimovian (315.2 to 303.7 million years ago)

facts.statement: The parent group of Iniopteryx is the family Iniopterygidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Iniopterygidae

facts.statement: There are 14 recorded fossil occurrences of Iniopteryx in the Paleobiology Database.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 14

facts.statement: The geological sites where Iniopteryx fossils were found are considered Konservat-Lagerstätten, meaning the fossils are exceptionally well preserved.
facts.quote: These sites are considered Konservat-Lagerstätten, meaning that fossils collected from the site are exceptionally well preserved.

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that Iniopteryx and related iniopterygians were visitors to basin environments rather than permanent residents.
facts.quote: Iniopteryx and other iniopterygians may have been open-ocean visitors to these basin environments, rather than full-time residents.
